text: In those days, when there was no king in Israel, a certain Levite living in the remote hill country of Ephraim took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.
But his concubine was unfaithful to him and left him for her father's house in Bethlehem of Judah, and she stayed there four whole months.

versions.text: But his concubine was unfaithful to him and left him for her father's house in Bethlehem of Judah, and she stayed there four months.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew idiom yamim arba'ah chodashim ("days, four months") signals a full span of time; "four whole months" captures the emphasis and reads naturally aloud.

text: Then her husband set out after her to speak tenderly to her and bring her back. He had his servant with him and a pair of donkeys. She brought him into her father's house, and when the young woman's father saw him, he welcomed him gladly.
His father-in-law, the young woman's father, pressed him to stay, so he remained with him three days; they ate and drank and spent the nights there.
On the fourth day they rose early in the morning, and the man got up to go. But the young woman's father said to his son-in-law, "Have a bite of bread to strengthen yourself, and then you can go."
So the two of them sat down and ate and drank together. Then the young woman's father said to the man, "Please, stay the night and enjoy yourself."
When the man got up to leave, his father-in-law urged him again, so he stayed the night there.
He rose early on the fifth morning to go, but the young woman's father said, "Strengthen yourself first, and wait until the day declines." So the two of them ate.

Then the man got up to go, he and his concubine and his servant, but his father-in-law, the young woman's father, said to him, "Look, the day is fading toward evening. Stay the night. See, the day is nearly over. Spend the night here and enjoy yourself. Tomorrow you can rise early for your journey and go home."
But the man would not stay the night. He got up and left, and came to a point opposite Jebus—that is, Jerusalem—with his pair of saddled donkeys and his concubine.
As they neared Jebus, the day was almost gone, and the servant said to his master, "Come, let us turn aside to this city of the Jebusites and spend the night there."
But his master said to him, "We will not turn aside into a foreign city where there are no Israelites. We will go on to Gibeah."
He said to his servant, "Come, let us reach one of these places and spend the night in Gibeah or Ramah."
So they went on their way, and the sun set on them as they came near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin.
They turned aside there to spend the night in Gibeah. He went in and sat down in the city square, but no one took them into his house for the night.
Then an old man came in from his work in the field at evening. He was from the hill country of Ephraim and was living in Gibeah, though the men of the place were Benjaminites.
He looked up and saw the traveler in the city square, and the old man asked, "Where are you going, and where do you come from?"

He answered him, "We are traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to the remote hill country of Ephraim. That is where I am from. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am going to the house of the LORD,* but no one has taken me into his house. [*Footnote: Some ancient witnesses read "to my house."]

versions.text: He answered him, "We are traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to the remote hill country of Ephraim. That is where I am from. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am going to the house of the LORD, but no one has taken me into his house.
versions.explanation: A brief footnote noting the well-known ancient variant ("to my house") would help readers, since the Levite in fact heads home in the following narrative.

text: We have straw and fodder for our donkeys, and bread and wine for myself, for your servant woman, and for the young man who is with your servants. We lack nothing."

versions.text: We have straw and fodder for our donkeys, and bread and wine for myself, your servant woman, and the young man with us. We lack nothing."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has the humble self-reference "with your servants," which the rendering "with us" flattens; restoring it preserves the deferential tone of the speech.

text: "Peace to you," said the old man. "Let me take care of whatever you need—only do not spend the night in the square."
So he brought him into his house and fed the donkeys. Then they washed their feet and ate and drank.

While they were enjoying themselves, the men of the city—worthless men—surrounded the house, pounding on the door. They shouted to the old man who owned the house, "Bring out the man who came into your house, so we can have our way with him!"
The owner of the house went out to them and said, "No, my brothers, do not do such an evil thing. This man is a guest in my house; do not commit this outrage.
Here is my virgin daughter and his concubine. Let me bring them out. Violate them and do to them whatever you please, but do not commit such an outrage against this man."
But the men would not listen to him. So the man seized his concubine and pushed her out to them. They raped her and abused her all night until morning, and let her go as dawn was breaking.
At daybreak the woman came and collapsed at the door of the man's house where her master was, and lay there until it was light.
When her master got up in the morning and opened the doors of the house to go on his way, there lay his concubine at the doorway of the house, her hands on the threshold.
He said to her, "Get up, let us go," but there was no answer. So he put her on his donkey and set out for home.
When he reached his house, he took a knife, took hold of his concubine, cut her limb by limb into twelve pieces, and sent them throughout all the territory of Israel.
Everyone who saw it said, "Nothing like this has ever happened or been seen from the day the Israelites came up out of the land of Egypt until this day. Think about it, take counsel, and speak!"

versions.text: Everyone who saw it said, "Nothing like this has ever happened or been seen from the day the Israelites came up out of Egypt until now. Consider it, take counsel, and speak."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads "from the land of Egypt" (מארץ מצרים); adding "the land of" restores the full phrase and gives the sentence a fuller oral cadence. Likewise "until this day" renders עד היום הזה more literally and balances the parallel with "from the day." The closing imperatives are a call to action, so an exclamation mark helps the reader deliver them with the urgency of the Hebrew.
